text: Always use a clean syringe and needle. Subcutaneous injection: given under the skin, used for products like Ivermectin and FMD vaccine. Intramuscular injection: the most common route; must be done smoothly since repeated injections over several days require the animal not to become needle-shy — oily long-acting antibiotics (often 20–30 ml) take time to inject fully, so the animal must be handled safely and calmly. Intravenous injection: used for large volumes or when a very fast response is needed; always check whether a given medicine is approved for IV use, and this route requires proper restraint/handling. Oral treatment: used for de-worming drugs or traditional medicines, done smoothly to prevent the animal spitting the dose out (wasting it) and, especially with large volumes, to avoid the product going down the trachea into the lungs. Intra-uterine medication: after delivery, retained placenta fragments often remain in the uterus and cause infection; placing 2–3 antibiotic boluses (about 10 g each, often TMP+Sulfa) helps prevent endometritis, a cause of repeat breeding and infertility. Intra-mammary treatment: not yet common in Cambodia; delivers antibiotic directly into the udder's cisterns and alveoli to fight mastitis infection, mainly used in dairy cattle. Eye drops: for heavy eye discharge, eyes turning white, or eyes kept closed, an antibiotic eye drop (e.g. gentamicin) speeds recovery and prevents lasting eye damage.
